answer.rationale: c2 confirms that the low-cost vendor has historically delivered accurate invoicing and quick onboarding, while c6 shows that multi-year commitments with the incumbent have unlocked meaningful unit cost reductions without eroding service scope. These two facts together strongly support pursuing aggressive term renegotiation on the expiring primary contract — leveraging the credible alternative (the low-cost vendor) to extract volume pricing and better payment terms from the incumbent, as c4 further validates that the incumbent can move on both price and terms when pressed. Renewing on status quo terms won't meet the 18% mandate; switching outright introduces migration risk against a 94%-utilization line with no buffer; adding a second source is valuable but addresses resilience rather than the cost reduction mandate; deferring forfeits the negotiation window before the contract expires in 14 days. Negotiating terms targets the primary objective — minimizing TCO without increasing delivery risk — since the incumbent relationship remains stable and the alternative vendor provides credible leverage.
